title: Where do you want me to look? Project 0 becomes three scenes, then four pages
introduction: This week was crit week. On Tuesday, Boyd spent the entire lesson teaching us how to conduct a critique; after class, he took a look at my ‘Project 0’ page and gave me a piece of advice that completely transformed the whole project. On Wednesday, I redesigned the page to feature three scenes. The critique session took place on Thursday, and on Friday we went on a day trip to Bristol for the Repair Festival. For the first six minutes of Tuesday’s lesson, Boyd spent his time helping everyone book train tickets: the 7.18 am service from Winchester, returning that same evening, where Teresa’s team would meet us. He booked my ticket for me personally. This was the first time I’d left Winchester since arriving here.
related_work:
Boyd taught us Liz Lerman’s Critical Response Process [1]. The process consists of four steps: first, the audience members express their interpretations of the work (what they found brilliant, what left a lasting impression); next, the artist poses a question; then, the audience members ask neutral questions; finally, personal opinions may only be expressed with the artist’s consent. The rule that made the greatest impression on me was that everyone must engage with every presenter: ‘Better to be wrong than to remain silent’. We practised using Boyd’s AR glasses. I said they looked ‘cute’, so he asked me why I thought they were cute. I had to point out the blue colour scheme and the style. Pointing out which design elements really work is far more difficult than it sounds.

We then practised in pairs. I was paired with Sam, who was building a small handheld games console. I told him it is small and you can really play it, you could take it on the train, and it could replace a board game; but if nobody tells you in advance, it is hard to see what the object is. When he asked about the ‘AI’ button, I admitted frankly that my English wasn’t good enough to be certain I’d fully understood the answer, and that the information box seemed a bit large for such a small screen. He said he’d make some updates. Offering advice that the other person can actually use feels far better than simply saying ‘that’s good’.

The crit is graded half on technique (the code, the choice between sprite sheet and transform, the colours, how it works on different screen sizes, how AI was used) and half on meaning (how the research leads to the story). So I re-examined my sources of information. At the end of my page, I cited a fact from Material Focus: in the UK, millions of disposable e-cigarettes are still thrown into the bin every week, and their batteries cause over a thousand fires a year in refuse collection vehicles and waste treatment facilities [2].
method:
After class, I showed Boyd my page. He said the content was fine, but the layout was unbalanced: ‘The text and images are the same size. Where do you want me to look? Make this one really big. It looks too scattered at the moment.’ He was right. All the elements on my page were the same size, so there was nothing to guide the eye. That was the most important thing I learnt this week.

On Tuesday evening, I was busy redrawing every section in black and white; on Wednesday, I worked on the storyboard, tracing the character and drawing the three scenes; on Wednesday evening, I drew the fourth page and wired up the language-model call; so by Thursday morning, I was still tweaking the frames. So I split this page into three scenes and placed them in the same HTML file. Scene One: You take apart an e-cigarette and read up on each component. Scene Two: You meet someone. Six panels tell the whole story (ten cigarettes a day, quitting, a ‘healthier’ e-cigarette, the first puff, three thousand puffs a day, unable to stop), with each panel corresponding to a line of text, followed by a button. Each click represents one puff: the page briefly switches to black and white, smoke drifts out, the battery level drops, and the mood rises and then falls along the mood curve. When the battery runs out, the person throws the e-cigarette away. Scene Three: the discarded e-cigarettes pile up; when the number reaches five, the pile catches fire. The ‘Back’ and ‘Next’ buttons in the corners allow you to switch between scenes in any order.

The second change concerns colour, and I must be honest with myself about this. In the first draft, I assigned different colours to each section simply to distinguish them from one another. There was no design rationale behind this; the colours were chosen at random. Boyd once said that we need artistic considerations, not just functionality. So now the entire page is in black and white, with the flames at the end being the only splash of colour on the page. This way, only one element stands out, which is exactly what he asked for. I saved the colour version in a backup folder and used a small script to create the black-and-white version; the script fills each section with black whilst retaining a one-pixel-wide white outline.

For the character, I designed eight action storyboards: holding a packet of cigarettes, discarding the packet, holding an e-cigarette, raising the e-cigarette, smoking and smiling, looking down whilst smoking, smoking with a blank expression, and discarding the e-cigarette. I used an AI-generated image as a reference to design the poses, then traced the keyframe (333×128, 1,314 pixels in total) pixel by pixel in Piskel, and used this as the basis to construct the remaining seven frames, as only the hands, face and held objects change between adjacent frames. These eight frames were integrated into a two-pixel-wide sprite strip, allowing the character to align perfectly with elements such as the parts, smoke and flames, which are all my own pixel drawings.
results_discussion:
This technique is the same as last week’s, but has been applied to a new scenario. Switching between scenes simply involves adding or removing a class: CSS hides all sections using display: none, whilst the section with the ‘on’ class is displayed. The ‘Back’ and ‘Next’ buttons call the same function, passing in the previous or the next number. The character strip works in a similar way to the smoke and flame sprite sheets: the background width is eight times that of the box, and a CSS variable, --f, picks the frame; JavaScript merely alters this value. The effect of the e-cigarette falling is achieved through a CSS transform transition, just like the effect of the sections moving outwards in the first scene. The flashing effect requires just one line of code: body.flash { filter: invert(1); }.

There are two aspects here that are entirely new to me. The mood curve is driven by setInterval: every half second, the mood sinks slightly towards the bottom, and this bottom level drops with every puff; consequently, the more one vapes, the lower the mood eventually becomes. The curve itself is drawn on the canvas using lineTo. The pile of discarded e-cigarettes, on the other hand, uses createElement: JavaScript generates a new image each time, assigns it the ‘dead’ class, and then CSS causes it to fall.

I also discovered a bug that gave me a new insight into the order of execution. I added a shortcut so that index.html#pile would jump directly to the final scene. On my first attempt, the scene was blank because the jump command was executed at the start of the file, whilst the script had not yet located the required elements. Once I moved those two lines of code to the end of the file, the problem was resolved. The script executes from top to bottom; you cannot use an element’s name until it exists.

My personal exercise this week has been the act of tracing itself. Although tracing by hand, frame by frame and pixel by pixel, is slow, it is the only way for me to truly understand how lines are transformed into a grid, and it is also the reason why the character does not look like a photograph pasted onto a pixelated page.

Thursday: the crit

From Wednesday to Thursday, these three scenes expanded to four pages, with a menu at the top: Start, Inside, Use, Thirty Years (Images 9–12). The fourth page is a new addition. On the left are the cobalt miners from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, accompanied by a fact from RAID and CAJJ [3]; whilst the right-hand side shows the same person ageing over the years, with discarded e-cigarettes piling up, transitioning from a state of health to one of exhaustion. The brief stipulated that a language model should form a central component; consequently, on the second and fourth pages, it is possible to pose questions to a small model (Ollama) running locally on my laptop, which responds based on the facts presented on the page. Each page features a Restart button, as participants often wished to go back during the crit.

The specific arrangements for the crit were as follows: eight minutes per person, with five minutes for the presentation and three minutes for feedback; whilst each person was speaking, the whole class would write down statements, questions and comments on the shared NodeNogg board, tagging the speaker’s name. I was second to speak, after Cecilia. In the first half, I used slides (explaining why I chose e-cigarettes, the five sections and their related facts, the pixel art style, why I switched to a black-and-white colour scheme, and why one page expanded into four), followed by a demonstration of the live website. For each page, I tried to explain how it worked in a single sentence: JavaScript changes a value, and CSS displays a different frame; JavaScript adds a class, and CSS moves that section using the transform property; the mood line consists of points drawn on the canvas. Five minutes wasn’t enough to show the code, so I pointed this out and moved on with my explanation.

The feedback I received was as follows: one student remarked that the visual presentation was engaging and that the content regarding the product was meaningful, as it helped them gain a deeper understanding of it; Boyd asked whether the content itself was clear, and the answer was affirmative. Another student commented that it was a major project and that I had clearly put a great deal of effort into it. Boyd’s own assessment was: ‘There are many things that are clear and striking. The aesthetic is working very well. I think it was smart to move to a clean black and white line drawing, because it helped us really focus on your message.’ As time ran out before the question round could begin, questions regarding my work will be moved to NodeNogg. The decision to adopt a black-and-white style was made on Wednesday after I heard his comment on Tuesday, so that one sentence from Tuesday went all the way through to the crit.

Inspiration I drew from other presentations: Cecilia’s electric toothbrush, where Boyd pointed out that the combination of pixel art and modern typography demonstrated that the artist had made a conscious choice; the charger website, where the AI poses a follow-up question for every fact presented, which Boyd described as a good use of the model, as it prompts reflection rather than merely providing information; the smartwatch controlled by camera-based gestures, which he described as a shift from ‘learning about a thing’ to ‘learning through a thing’; the torch story game, where a fellow student suggested adding a highlighted button to indicate where to click, which was a useful suggestion for me too; and Sam’s games console, where everyone agreed that every section was clear and straightforward. The headphones and the game controller ran out of time, so they will receive their feedback next week.

The English was the most difficult part for me. Whilst I could explain the functions on each page, I was unable to fully explain the reasoning behind them; when I couldn’t recall a particular word, I had to rely on the sequence of the slides to fill in the gaps. The presentation itself went smoothly. What I would change is my approach to planning the week. I underestimated the workload for ‘Project 0’: the advice I received on Tuesday meant I needed a new structure, new illustrations and a new character, and all this work piled up on Tuesday and Wednesday, so I was still tweaking the frames on Wednesday evening instead of practising. Next time, I will estimate the workload in advance.

Friday: Bristol

On Friday, I took the 7.18 am train to Bristol to attend the Repair Festival, changing at Basingstoke and Reading on the way. The morning workshop took place at City Hall. A consultant specialising in creating digital twins of buildings began by asking us what we understood by the term ‘digital twin’. His explanation comprised three parts: a physical entity (not necessarily a building), its virtual model, and the link between the two, so that any changes occurring in the physical entity are simultaneously reflected in the digital model. He said that whilst people often refer to it as a ‘copy’, it is not a copy but rather a representation. It can be as simple as a photograph of a room, or as complex as point clouds, BIM models and real-time sensors; he described these as ‘low-fidelity to high-fidelity’ representations. I listened to the talk using the real-time translation function on my mobile phone, and it worked better than I had expected.

What struck me most was his list of what the model leaves out. The scanned wall is merely a surface, but the actual wall consists of bricks, insulation and plaster, as well as a specific brand of paint (which is due to be repainted in a certain year), its U-value, date of construction, maintenance costs and a memory. Next come the trickier questions: which file format should be used? Who would maintain the digital twin? Who would own the data? Who would be able to use it? These are the same questions as in ‘Project 0’, except that the subject has shifted from an e-cigarette to a building: the clean, streamlined model obscures the true story of the materials. He showcased Ashton Court Mansion, scanned room by room using Matterport, and the former Marks & Spencer building in Broadmead, now known as Sparks and run by Artspace Lifespace while it waits for a buyer: the ground floor houses a repair café and a shop, whilst the further one ascends, right up to the roof, the more evident the signs of dereliction become [4].

We then scanned the room ourselves using LiDAR apps on our mobile phones (3D Scanner App and Polycam [5]). My scan produced a pink and blue point cloud, with holes where people had moved; Polycam converted this into a navigable mesh model in just five minutes (Images 13 to 15). This was my first 3D work based on a real location rather than a hand-drawn sketch, though it remains only a very rough twin: the room is really there, whilst the people are as insubstantial as ghosts. I took part in the entire morning session, from the lecture to the scanning.
conclusion_future_work: The website is hosted on GitHub Pages, and a link has been added to this portfolio. The only assignment this week is to provide feedback on NodeNogg by Tuesday; Boyd has indicated that he will introduce Project 1 next week. The main lesson I learnt this week is that hierarchy is a design decision, not a mere embellishment: each page focuses on a single key point, and the only colour appears at the end. Bristol added a second insight: a model is never the thing itself, and the essence of a story often lies in what it leaves out.
